opus-5.5.text:
I think we're heading toward a world where a lot more companies will have something that looks like an internal AI research function, but it won't necessarily look like a frontier lab. Most companies aren't going to pretrain their own foundation models, and they shouldn't. But there's this really interesting middle layer opening up, especially around reinforcement learning and post-training, where the barrier to entry has come down a lot.

What I find compelling is that the thing that's actually scarce isn't the base model anymore. It's the environment. It's knowing what good looks like for your particular task, having the tools and the data and the evaluation criteria that let you say "this rollout was better than that one." Companies sitting on deep domain expertise, whether that's legal workflows or chip design or customer support, already have a lot of the ingredients for building good RL environments. They just haven't historically thought of that knowledge as a training asset.

So I imagine it starting pretty modestly. A team builds really good evals for their product first, because you need those anyway. Then they realize those evals are basically reward functions, and if you wrap them in an environment with the right tools, you can start doing targeted fine-tuning or RL on open-weight models. Maybe you get a smaller model that's cheaper and better at your specific thing than a general-purpose frontier model. That's a real research capability, even if it's a handful of people.

The other piece is that I think open-source infrastructure matters a lot here. If every company has to reinvent the training stack, environment abstractions, and rollout infrastructure, only the biggest players will do it. If there are shared, composable tools, where you can plug your environment into a trainer and iterate quickly, then the research becomes about the interesting part: what are you teaching the model, and how do you know it learned it?

And culturally, it means treating this as an empirical, iterative discipline rather than a one-off project. Researchers who are comfortable looking at a lot of model outputs, noticing weird behaviors, reward hacking, things like that, and adjusting. That kind of taste is going to be one of the most valuable things a company can build in-house.

r002.rationale: The response says most companies should not pretrain foundation models and does not identify pretraining as an option for needs beyond text-in, text-out.

r003.rationale: It describes targeted fine-tuning or reinforcement learning on open-weight models for a company’s specific task.

r004.rationale: It says barriers to entry have fallen and that a task-specific model may be cheaper, but does not state that task-focused post-training is becoming cost-effective at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most companies shouldn't be trying to replicate what a frontier lab does. That's not the game. The game for most companies is figuring out what the frontier models can't quite do yet for their specific problem, and then closing that gap themselves.

And the thing that's changed in the last year or two is that the tools for doing that have gotten way more accessible. Like, reinforcement learning on top of an open model used to be this thing where you needed a dedicated infra team and a lot of patience just to get a run that didn't fall over. Now you've got frameworks where a couple of engineers can set up an environment, define a reward, and start getting signal in a week. That's a real shift. It means the barrier isn't compute or tooling anymore, it's mostly about whether you understand your own problem well enough to write down what good looks like.

So when I think about a company building a research capability, I actually think the first step isn't hiring a bunch of PhDs. It's building the evaluation muscle. Can you take the thing your business actually cares about and turn it into something measurable, something you can run a model against a thousand times and get a number? Because if you can do that, you've basically built an environment, and once you have an environment you can do RL on it, you can do data curation against it, you can compare models honestly. Most companies skip that step and go straight to fine-tuning on whatever data they have lying around, and then they can't tell if it helped.

The second thing is that I'd encourage people to think of it as applied research rather than fundamental research. You're not trying to discover a new architecture. You're trying to take techniques that are already published, that are already somewhat de-risked, and figure out how they behave on your data and your tasks. That's still genuinely research. There's a lot of unknowns in it. But it's a much more tractable kind of research, and the payoff is directly tied to the business.

And then the last piece, and this is the one I think people underrate, is that you want a tight loop between the people who understand the domain and the people running the experiments. Ideally they're the same people. The best setups I've seen are small teams, like three to five people, where someone really knows the problem, someone can write the training code, and they're just iterating fast. The worst setups are where there's a research org off to the side that gets handed a vague mandate and then has to go find a problem.

So, build evals, treat it as applied work, keep the team small and close to the problem. That's kind of my whole pitch.

r001.rationale: The response says most companies should not replicate a frontier lab; it does not predict that most AI companies will want their own research labs.

r002.rationale: It does not identify pre-training or discuss models beyond text-in, text-out.

r003.rationale: It describes applied research on company data and tasks, including reinforcement learning on an open model and fine-tuning, as ways to adapt models to specific problems.

r004.rationale: It says the tools have become more accessible and a small team can get signal quickly, but does not state that task-focused post-training is cost-effective at scale for suitable problems.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of companies will start by building the ability to evaluate models on the things they actually care about. Can you tell whether a model is doing a good job on your work? Can you run an experiment and reliably tell whether you made it better? That gives you a foundation for research.

From there, you can imagine a small team taking existing models and adapting them using the company’s own data and environments. They don’t necessarily need to train a foundation model from scratch. Their advantage is that they understand a particular problem, have access to examples of it, and can get feedback on what works.

The interesting transition is when that becomes a continuous process: you find failures, develop a hypothesis, train or modify the system, and measure the result. At that point, you’re developing a research capability, even if you didn’t start by setting out to build an AI lab.

r001.rationale: It says many companies may build evaluation and adaptation capabilities, but does not predict that most AI companies will want their own research labs.

r004.rationale: It does not say task-focused post-training is becoming cost-effective at scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of companies will start by building the ability to evaluate models on the things they actually care about. If you can tell whether a model is doing a good job on your problems, you have a foundation for improving it. You can experiment with different models, give them better tools and context, and eventually do more specialized training where it makes sense.

That creates a pretty natural path toward an internal research capability. You have people forming hypotheses, running experiments, and learning from failures, grounded in a domain the company understands well. You don’t necessarily need to start with a huge team training a general-purpose model. A small team with a clear problem and a reliable way to measure progress can do useful research, and grow from there.
